titulo.texto: Models of Alta Vista and La Quemada

frase_gancho.texto: Two sites on the northern frontier, shrunk to scale so you can take them in at a glance.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the cities of the farmers, we move on to the art of other peoples of the north, the hunters of Baja California. Look for a great wall with figures of people and animals painted on rock, mostly in red and black.

guion_corto.texto: Two models bring together, in miniature, two places on the northern frontier of Mesoamerica, both in Zacatecas. Alta Vista, in Chalchihuites, is a ceremonial center almost directly on the Tropic of Cancer. The corners of its buildings point to the four directions, and one of its halls has twenty-eight columns. La Quemada rises on a hill, with terraces, a wall, a hall of columns, a pyramid and a ball court. It was inhabited between the years 300 and 1200 AD. In its ruins there are traces of fire, and it is still not known for certain what happened. Seen together, the two sites remind us that, at the edge of the desert, there were also plazas, temples and people who watched the sky.

guion_largo.texto:
A model offers what no display case can: it lets you see an entire place from above. With Alta Vista and La Quemada, this helps a great deal, because these are sites that are understood through their layout. What matters is where the plazas are, which way the buildings face, and how you climb from one terrace to the next. With the two models in front of you, you can compare two ways of living at the edge of Mesoamerica.

Let’s begin with Alta Vista, in the Chalchihuites mountains. Manuel Gamio explored it in 1908, and from 1971 the archaeologist Charles Kelley directed excavations there for years. Its ceremonial center was built around the fifth century. Some studies propose that it was founded by priests linked to Teotihuacán, although that remains only a proposal. The corners of its plazas and buildings point to the four cardinal points, something uncommon in Mesoamerica. In addition, the place seems to have been chosen with care, because it forms a triangulation with three hills called Picacho Pelón, Chapín and Pedregoso.

Among its structures there is a hall with twenty-eight columns, in four rows of seven. It has been interpreted as a calendar, because of the twenty-eight days of a cycle of the Moon. In another part of the site there is a long corridor with adobe walls, called the labyrinth. It is said that at the equinox the first rays of the Sun enter through it. Even today, many people come to Alta Vista every spring to welcome the Sun.

In the hall of columns, an offering appeared with the remains of sacrificed people. Among its objects were four cups with an eagle and a serpent. They are decorated with the same technique as the [tubular vessel from Alta Vista](mna_s11_vaso_chalchihuites) that you saw at the beginning of this hall. According to the site museum, the eagle is the Sun conquering the serpent to control the rains and secure the harvest. In a place so close to the desert, rain was everything.

La Quemada is another story. It lies about fifty kilometers south of the city of Zacatecas, on a hill that overlooks the Malpaso valley. It was occupied between the years 300 and 1200, and it was one of the most important centers of its region. Its builders used slabs of rhyolite, a volcanic rock, bonded with mud, and they adapted the hill with terraces.

Let your eyes travel over its parts. There is a hall of columns of about forty meters by thirty, and a votive pyramid more than ten meters high. There is also a ball court and a wide causeway that starts from the plaza. To the north runs a wall about eight hundred meters long, which some specialists link to the defense of the place. And then there is the fire: in several spots there are traces of burning, and for that reason people speak of a violent end. But archaeologists have not been able to determine what happened.

Centuries ago, moreover, it was believed that La Quemada was Chicomóztoc, the place of the seven caves from which, according to tradition, the Nahua Peoples set out. You already know that name, because it appeared at the beginning of this hall. In 1615, the friar Juan de Torquemada placed the site on that migratory route. In 1780, the Jesuit Francisco Javier Clavijero identified it with Chicomóztoc. Today archaeologists treat that idea as an old speculation. Even so, it shows how much the site drew the attention of those who saw it in ruins.

Look at the two models and compare. Alta Vista seems designed to follow the Sun, and La Quemada, to dominate a valley. One speaks of calendars and rain, and the other, of power and fire. Both can be visited today, in Zacatecas, and from there it is easier to understand why Mesoamerica did not end at a line.

texto.Culture: Chalchihuites culture (Alta Vista) and regional center of the Malpaso valley (La Quemada)
texto.Period: Alta Vista, ceremonial center from approximately the 5th century AD; La Quemada, occupied between 300 and 1200 AD
texto.Origin: Alta Vista, Chalchihuites, and La Quemada, Villanueva, Zacatecas

texto.pregunta: Myth: North of the desert there were only nomad camps, with no plazas or temples.
texto.respuesta: Reality: In Zacatecas there were sites such as Alta Vista and La Quemada, with plazas, temples and halls of columns, and at La Quemada also a ball court.
